standard.title: Networks and network diagrams
standard.description: interpret networks and network diagrams used to represent relationships in practical situations and describe connectedness
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can describe position and location in 3 dimensions using coordinate systems (AC9M8SP03). They have not yet encountered network diagrams as a mathematical representation of relationships, nor worked with concepts of connectedness, edges, vertices, or graph-theoretic properties.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students interpret networks and network diagrams representing relationships in practical situations, describe connectedness, and apply Euler's formula to polyhedra represented as networks.

nodes.label: Network diagrams — structure and vocabulary
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the nodes and edges of a network diagram and explain what each represents in a given practical context.
nodes.minimum_width: Given a network diagram for a practical situation, identify the nodes (vertices) and edges; describe in plain language what each represents in the context.
nodes.typical_width: Interpret network diagrams for at least three different practical contexts (transport, social, ecological, technological); identify nodes and edges; describe what connectedness means in each context; distinguish directed from undirected networks where relevant.
wider: Represent First Nations Australians' kinship systems using network diagrams and explore the significance of the relationships to Country/Place encoded in the network

Investigate how a home network (LAN), social network, or electrical wiring network can be represented as a network diagram and use it to identify practical issues (e.g. single points of failure, router placement)

response_modes.reason: Network diagrams look structurally similar across contexts but encode very different relationships. Students who only interpret one type of network (e.g. transport) may not recognise that kinship systems, food webs and computer networks use the same mathematical object. Multiple contexts build generalised network thinking.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The kinship system context provides rich engagement — connecting a mathematical representation to a sophisticated cultural knowledge system — that goes beyond technical skill and develops genuine appreciation for networks as meaning-making structures.
success_criteria: Student correctly identifies nodes and edges in a network diagram and explains what each represents in context
Student describes connectedness — what it means for two nodes to be connected — in terms of the practical situation

nodes.label: Analysing connectedness
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse the connectedness of a network, identifying connected components, paths, and constraints such as traversability.
nodes.minimum_width: Determine whether a given network is connected (all nodes reachable from any starting node); identify a path between two specified nodes.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse connectedness in practical network contexts; identify connected vs disconnected networks; trace paths between nodes; investigate the Königsberg bridge problem as a classical example of traversability (Eulerian path); identify whether a network has an Eulerian path based on vertex degree.
wider: Investigate food web networks — identify producers, consumers and decomposers as node types; analyse what happens to the network if a key node is removed
Explore metabolic networks or other biological/chemical structures as graph representations and discuss what network properties reveal about the system

response_modes.reason: The Königsberg bridge problem and Eulerian path reasoning require systematic thinking about vertex degree — students need the odd-degree criterion explained, not just demonstrated. Explicit scaffolding of the reasoning prevents trial-and-error approaches.

success_criteria: Student correctly determines whether a given network is connected and justifies the answer
Student traces a valid path between two specified nodes in a network diagram

nodes.label: Polyhedra as networks and Euler's formula
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can represent a polyhedron as a network diagram and verify Euler's formula F + V = E + 2.
nodes.minimum_width: Draw the network representation of a simple polyhedron (e.g. cube, tetrahedron); count faces, vertices and edges; verify F + V = E + 2.
nodes.typical_width: Represent multiple polyhedra as network diagrams; verify Euler's formula for each; identify exterior and interior faces in the network representation; explain why the formula holds as a topological property rather than a geometric coincidence.
wider: Investigate how Euler's formula connects to planar graph theory and discuss which graphs can be drawn without edge crossings
Explore polyhedra with 'holes' (toruses) and investigate how Euler's formula changes for different topological structures

response_modes.reason: Representing polyhedra as networks integrates 3D spatial knowledge with graph theory — students must translate between a geometric object and its topological network representation. This is the cross-domain integration point of the descriptor.

success_criteria: Student correctly draws the network representation of a given polyhedron
Student verifies Euler's formula by correctly counting faces, vertices and edges
